The thirty second summary is this: there were three exploits published recently related to a security flaw in x86-type (i.e. modern consumer) CPUs. Two of them are called Spectre (-One and -Two,) the third is called Meltdown. They're all a big deal security-wise, but Spectre-1 is a relatively easy fix that costs nothing in performance. Spectre-2's impact depends on the design of the processor, but most people won't notice either way. Patching Meltdown, however, requires significantly slowing down the way the CPU executes instructions. AMD chips are vulnerable only to Spectre-1 and patches are already available across operating systems (though the official Windows patch has been crashing some systems, but that's on Microsoft not AMD.) ARM cpus like the one in your phone are vulnerable to Spectre-1 and -2, and not all devices have patches available yet. In terms of security, this is the biggest issue for that reason. Intel CPUs are also vulnerable to both Spectre attacks, but they also have the unique hardware flaw that makes them vulnerable to Meltdown. Intel has known about this for years (before the release of their last series of chips with this flaw) and patching it will cost a significant amount of performance for all users. Exactly how much depends on what you're doing, but worst real-world case seems to be about a 30% slowdown.
